analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated investigator inside USDA to prosecute unfair meatpacking and poultry practices.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters inside the Department of Agriculture. That office would investigate and prosecute meatpackers and live poultry dealers that violate the Packers and Stockyards Act, a century-old law meant to keep livestock markets fair, and it could bring civil cases directly instead of waiting on the Justice Department. Four big meatpacking companies process the large majority of American beef and poultry, so ranchers and smaller processors say they face few real alternatives when prices paid at the farm gate are squeezed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ranchers, poultry growers, and smaller meat processors who sell livestock into a market dominated by a handful of large packers, plus consumers who may face fairer competition upstream.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a permanent office headed by a senior career investigator that must use every available tool, including subpoenas, to investigate and prosecute Packers and Stockyards Act violations by packers and live poultry dealers [S2] [S3].

Gives the investigator independent authority to bring civil or administrative actions against packers and live poultry dealers, removing the current bottleneck of routing every case through the Justice Department [S2] [S3].

Requires the office to coordinate with the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, and USDA's own enforcement units, and to maintain a staff of specialized attorneys, so competition cases in the food sector are pursued continuously rather than episodically [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking and poultry processing companies, which would face a dedicated enforcement arm using subpoenas and civil suits under a law written to police their market conduct.

drawbacks.text: The bill expands federal enforcement against meatpackers without new funding or dedicated staff in the legislation itself, so enforcement would depend on future appropriations, which often does not materialize [S3].

A dedicated investigator can only act against entities regulated under the Packers and Stockyards Act, so much of the retail food supply chain and other antitrust problems in the sector remain outside its reach [S3].

Stronger enforcement against packers is a good-faith disagreement point: the industry argues that consolidation and vertical integration lower consumer prices and that added litigation risk raises costs for processors, which could be passed back through the supply chain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill creates a focused enforcement office aimed at one of the most concentrated industries in the country, with direct civil enforcement powers that today sit largely with agencies that have not prioritized these cases. The main design weaknesses are that it adds no dedicated funding and its reach stops at the packer gate, leaving retail-level food prices to other enforcers. Those are modest limits relative to what the office could do.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, with a bipartisan group of ten cosponsors, four Republicans and six Democrats [S4] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day, and it never left that committee [S5].

The only related action in the entire two-year Congress was a Banking Committee hearing in May 2024 whose record was printed as S.Hrg. 118-646; the bill itself never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking and poultry processors are better off, because no dedicated enforcement office was created to pursue Packers and Stockyards Act cases against them during this Congress.

for.name: Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of ten cosponsors.

against.name: Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup on the bill she had cosponsored, leaving it in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Large meatpackers and poultry processors
against.what_they_did: Opposed dedicated Packers and Stockyards Act enforcement and a special investigator outside direct Agriculture Department control.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split across both parties, with ten cosponsors including four of the 49 Senate Republicans and six of the 48 Senate Democrats, and no roll-call vote was ever held.

industries.industry: Meatpacking and poultry processing (packers and live poultry dealers)
industries.note: The bill targets these companies directly with subpoena-backed investigations and civil enforcement under the Packers and Stockyards Act. A handful of large firms dominate livestock buying, so dedicated enforcement narrows their room to squeeze the prices they pay farmers.

industries.industry: Livestock producers (cattle ranchers and poultry growers)
industries.note: Growers selling into a market dominated by a few large packers would gain an enforcer dedicated to policing unfair trade practices, with better prices passed along through the supply chain.
Enforcement aimed at packer practices that disadvantage smaller competitors would support a more diverse processing sector, which also affects farmers' choice of where to sell.
